summary.title: The Mirage of Optimizing Training Policies: Monotonic Inference Policies as the Real Objective for LLM Reinforcement Learning

details: Training-inference mismatch in LLM RL (separate training engine vs. inference/rollout engine assign different probabilities to the same trajectory even with synchronized parameters) causes an objective misalignment: improving the training policy does not imply improving the inference policy actually deployed.
Prior remedies (ratio corrections, token filtering, LR decay, precision fixes) only reduce mismatch on the training side and leave the objective itself misaligned.

MIPI principle: take monotonic improvement of the inference policy, J(mu_{k+1}) - J(mu_k), as the RL objective, decomposed into post-update inference gap + training-side update + pre-update inference gap.

MIPU algorithm realizing MIPI in two steps: (1) a sampler-referenced policy update whose importance weight and advantage are anchored at the rollout (inference) policy while the proximal clip stays on the current training-side update ratio; (2) after synchronization, estimate the post-update inference gap on validation rollouts and accept the candidate only if the proxy exceeds a tolerance, otherwise roll back trainer, optimizer state, and inference engine to the previous checkpoint.
Qwen3-4B (trained on 1491 filtered DeepMath-103K problems) and Qwen3-1.7B (5759 filtered DAPO-Math-17k problems); filtering keeps non-trivial, non-saturated success rates.
High-mismatch regime induced deliberately by FP8-quantized rollout; ROLL framework with Megatron trainer and vLLM inference on 8xH100.
GRPO-style training: group size 8, batch size 64, lr 1e-6, response length 8192, dual-clip loss with eps=0.2, KL coef 0.001.
Step 1 uses token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS): mismatch weight w = pi_k/mu_k truncated at w_max=2, multiplied onto the dual-clipped GRPO objective.
Step 2 proxy: negative expectation over validation rollouts of (length-normalized sequence ratio pi_{k+1}/mu_{k+1}) times group-relative advantage under mu_{k+1}; accept if proxy >= -c.
Dynamic tolerance c linearly annealed over first 100 steps (4e-3 to 1e-3 for 1.7B; 1e-3 to 0 for 4B).
Vanilla GRPO baseline, MIS (token-level masking of tokens with mismatch weight > 2), and LR-decay (halving lr every ~234-249 steps down to a floor).
Infrastructure-level mismatch remedies deliberately excluded as orthogonal.
Step-1 variants compared in appendix: PPO-IS (clip full trainer-to-sampler ratio), Vanilla-IS (untruncated correction weight), TIS.
Five math reasoning benchmarks: MATH-500, AIME24, AMC23, Minerva, OlympiadBench; pass@1, avg@16 on AIME24/AMC23; eval temperature 0.7.
Stability judged by whether performance collapses or sharply degrades during continued training after reaching a peak.
Diagnostics: inference-training K3-KL on rollout tokens, post-update gap proxy, rollback rate over 100-step moving windows.
Baseline vs. Step 1 only vs. Step 2 only vs. full MIPU on Qwen3-4B FP8 rollout.
Random rollback control rejecting updates at ~70% probability, matched to the observed Step-2-only rollback rate.
Sensitivity sweep over acceptance tolerance c including stricter-than-zero (c<0) settings.

key_findings.finding: Framing LLM RL as monotonic improvement of the inference policy and implementing it via sampler-referenced updates plus inference-gap-gated acceptance yields both higher accuracy and stable training under high mismatch.
key_findings.evidence: Under FP8-quantized rollout, MIPU reaches best average pass@1 of 66.71% on Qwen3-4B (vs. 64.42 GRPO, 63.42 MIS, 65.66 LR-decay) and 53.97% on Qwen3-1.7B (vs. 50.86/51.73/52.23), and is the only method marked stable; training curves show baselines peaking then degrading while MIPU's score trajectory stays flat.

key_findings.finding: The two steps address distinct failure modes and are complementary: candidate quality alone or acceptance filtering alone is insufficient.
key_findings.evidence: Qwen3-4B ablation: Step 1 only reaches 65.36 average, Step 2 only drops to 62.81 (below the 64.42 baseline, e.g. AMC23 falls to 75.00), while the full method reaches 66.71; Step 2 alone prevents collapse but mostly retains the previous inference policy when baseline candidates are poor, whereas Step 1 alone accepts every synchronized candidate and accumulates mismatch fluctuations.

key_findings.finding: Step 2's benefit comes from the inference-gap signal, not from merely applying fewer updates.
key_findings.evidence: A random rollback control rejecting 67.0% of candidates (more conservative than Step 2's 53.5% in the same window) still collapses after a transient peak, while Step 2 maintains a stable score trajectory.

key_findings.finding: The post-update inference gap proxy carries structured, mismatch-relevant signal rather than noise, and its acceptance threshold must be calibrated rather than made maximally strict.
key_findings.evidence: Qwen3-1.7B shows both larger inference-training K3-KL and larger, more volatile proxy magnitude than Qwen3-4B; both models show mismatch growing and the proxy shifting upward over training, motivating an annealed tolerance. Overly strict acceptance (c<0) enters persistent rollback after ~280 steps and plateaus at lower score.

key_findings.finding: Among sampler-referenced update forms, factorizing the trainer-to-sampler ratio and truncating only the pre-update mismatch weight is the best Step-1 choice.
key_findings.evidence: On Qwen3-4B FP8 rollout, PPO-IS (clipping the full pi/mu ratio) exhibits a much larger clip ratio and fails to sustain an upward learning trajectory despite lower measured KL; Vanilla-IS with unbounded correction shows large gradient-norm spikes; TIS gives the best stability-performance trade-off.
